improvement_notes: Add one compact diagram or sentence distinguishing a single gear mesh from a complete gearbox, since real robot transmissions commonly include multiple stages and additional shaft losses.

Make the motor operating-point limitation even more prominent immediately before the first numerical calculation; beginners may otherwise interpret the stated speed and torque as simultaneously guaranteed motor specifications.

The lesson is highly complete but somewhat long for a foundational class. Consider shortening repeated cautions about traction, motor operating point, and model boundaries, especially after the Python lab and again in Common Mistakes.

Clarify that the displayed wheel-rim force is a torque-based estimate and not necessarily a static maximum force, since acceleration, motor torque-speed behavior, and controller current limits are excluded.

The generated visuals support the mathematics well, but the Real Robot Connection would benefit from one authentic photograph of an exposed compact robot gearbox or motor-to-wheel transmission, with a caption identifying motor shaft, gear stages, wheel shaft, bearings, and packaging constraints.

In the optional two-stage example, explicitly state that the quoted combined efficiency of 0.80 is an assumed overall efficiency, not the efficiency of each stage; the final sentence implies this, but a short numerical comparison would reinforce the point.

linkedin.title: Robotics Class 9: How Gears Trade Speed for Strength
linkedin.description: A practical lesson on gear ratios, torque, efficiency, wheel force, and Python-based gear selection for RoboRover’s next design challenge.
linkedin.commentary:
A robot motor may spin quickly and still struggle to move a wheel up a ramp. The transmission between them changes the trade.

In Professor OS Class 9, students use RoboRover to investigate:

• How tooth counts determine a reduction ratio
• Why reducing speed can increase output torque
• How efficiency changes an ideal calculation
• Why wheel radius and traction limit real force
• How Python can compare competing gear choices

The lesson moves from a 12-tooth driver and 36-tooth driven gear to a practical climbing decision. Students calculate speed, torque, and wheel-rim force, then test their reasoning in an interactive gear-selection challenge.

Try the lab: choose a transmission for a rover that must climb while remaining fast enough for useful movement. Then ask what the simplified model leaves out—motor heating, current limits, slipping, and gearbox losses.
